tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. - a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Every deletion, no matter how it starts, reduces to "unlink a node with at most one child."

STEP 0 — reduce to the base case:

      -> N must be a leaf (a red node's children are NIL/black-only, and if N had
         one child that child would be black, which would already break black-height
         before you touched anything — so a red N can't have exactly one child).

         would already have broken invariant 3 before deletion).

      -> C now carries exactly the black N used to carry. No debt created.
      -> DONE, no sibling-based fixup loop should run. (Case 6, Figure 8 — the
         "side door" case that two-children reduction walks into constantly.)

  if N is BLACK and has zero children (a black leaf):
      -> the slot left behind is "doubly black" (owes one black node). This is
         the only case that needs the real fixup loop. Go to STEP 2.

  Look at the doubly-black slot's SIBLING (S) and PARENT (P).

  if S is RED:
      -> (forces P black, S's children black, by rule 4/5).
      -> rotate S up over P, swap colors (P <-> S's old color).
      -> NOTHING is fixed yet — this is a pure reshuffle, no black-height changed

         1-for-1 between P and S).

         red child = new red-red violation).

         relocated red node becomes the missing black.
      -> TERMINAL. Debt fully paid in this one step, regardless of P's color.
         Never climbs further. (Case 4.)

      -> no red material anywhere nearby to rotate with — rotating black nodes
         here only moves an existing black around, it can't manufacture a new one.
      -> recolor S red (strips a black from S's branch too, so both branches under

            to P. Re-run STEP 2 with P's slot as the new deficient node. (Case 3b —
            this is the case that climbs, possibly to the root.)

  if the debt climbs all the way to the root: it just disappears — a root with
  no black debt above it needs nothing further, black-height simply dropped by one
  uniformly, which is legal (invariant 3 only requires paths to AGREE, not a fixed
  absolute count).

message.content: Exactly when do doomed pointers get freed?

rendered.content:
<system-reminder>

</system-reminder>

content.text:
Precise timeline, per case — "doomed" meaning the key/value belonging to the **logical entry for the requested key**, which is not always the same physical node as the one that gets unlinked.

## Case A: `z` has ≤1 child (`n == z`, `free_own_payload = true`)

The doomed key/value *are* `z`'s own fields, and they're freed **last**, after the structural change:

1. `transplant(t, n, child)` — structural unlink happens first. `n` (== `z`) is now off-tree, but the local pointer `n` still holds a valid address; its `key`/`value` fields are untouched.
2. `rb_free(n->key)` — doomed key freed.
3. `if (t->value_free) t->value_free(n->value)` — doomed value freed.
4. `rb_free(n)` — the now-empty struct itself freed last, after both its payload pointers are already gone (they're dangling inside a soon-to-be-freed struct, never dereferenced again).

## Case B: `z` has two children (`n == y`, `free_own_payload = false`)

Here the doomed key/value are `z`'s **original** fields (before overwrite) — and they're freed **first**, before anything structural happens at all:

1. `rb_free(z->key)` — doomed key freed, immediately upon locating `y = tree_min(z->right)`, before `y`'s child is even computed, before any transplant.
2. `if (t->value_free) t->value_free(z->value)` — doomed value freed, same moment.
3. `z->key = y->key; z->value = y->value;` — transfer, not a free. `y`'s original key/value pointers are now aliased into `z`.
4. `transplant(t, y, child)` — structural unlink of `y`, later.
5. `rb_free(n)` where `n == y` — frees **only the `struct rb_node` itself**. `free_own_payload` is `false`, so the `rb_free(n->key)`/`value_free(n->value)` block is skipped entirely — `y`'s (now `z`'s) key/value are never touched here.

## The asymmetry, stated plainly

The doomed pointers are freed **before** the structural unlink in the two-children case, and **after** it in the ≤1-child case. That's safe — freeing a heap string or calling `value_free` never depends on tree topology, only on nothing else still holding that pointer — but it means there are two different "doomed-free" call sites in the function, not one shared one. `y`'s own original key/value allocations are **never freed by this call at all**; they're relabeled as `z`'s and will be freed whenever `z`'s entry is eventually deleted or the tree is destroyed. Only the empty `y` struct dies now.

Still no edits to `src/rbtree.c` or the test file — this is answering your question against the pseudocode from the last plan, not a revision.

message.content: after moving/copying a successor's key and value, are there temporarily 2 nodes claiming the same allocation?

content.text:
Yes — from the moment of the copy until `y`'s struct is freed, `z->key`/`z->value` and `y->key`/`y->value` hold **identical pointer values** (same heap allocations), simultaneously. That's real aliasing, not a hypothetical.

**Exact window:** opens at `z->key = y->key; z->value = y->value;` (before `child` is even computed, before `transplant`). It stays open through `transplant(t, y, child)` — at that point `y` is structurally off the tree, but its `key`/`value` fields are still sitting there, still equal to `z`'s. The window closes only when `rb_free(n)` runs on `y`'s struct at the very end — after that, there's nothing left to alias with.

**Why it's safe rather than a double-free waiting to happen:** aliasing two pointer *values* is harmless on its own; what would actually break the single-owner contract is calling `rb_free`/`value_free` through *both* fields. That's exactly what `free_own_payload = false` prevents — it's a guard specifically for this window, ensuring `y`'s copy of those pointers is never used to free anything. Only `z`'s copy is ever a live "owning" reference from this function's perspective; `y`'s copy is inert stale data riding along in a struct that's about to be freed as raw memory.

**The failure mode this guards against:** if that flag were ever dropped or the two `if (free_own_payload)` branches got merged during a refactor, you'd free `y->key`/`y->value` — which are the *same allocations* `z` now depends on — leaving `z->key`/`z->value` dangling. The tree would look fine until the next `rb_find`/`rb_delete`/`rb_destroy` touched that key, at which point it's a use-after-free (and a second free at the real end-of-life, so also a double-free). `free_own_payload` exists precisely because two structs transiently share these pointers and only one of them is allowed to ever call `free` on them.

Still not touching `src/rbtree.c` — flag if you want this window narrowed (e.g., nulling `y->key`/`y->value` defensively right after the copy) or if you're satisfied the guard-flag approach is sufficient.

message.content: does it still work if there is no intermediate parent? trace it

content.text:
Concrete trace using the tree we already verified empirically (`d,b,f,a,c,e,g`): delete `"f"`, where `f`'s two children are `e` (left) and `g` (right, a leaf). Here `y = tree_min(z->right) = g`, and `g`'s parent **is** `z` (`f`) directly — no node `p` sits between them.

```
Before:           f(B)
                 /    \
              e(R)   g(R)   <- z=f, z->right=g, g is a leaf (child=NULL)
```

**Step-by-step:**

1. `z = find_node(t, "f")` → the `f` node.
2. `z->left && z->right` both non-NULL → two-children branch.
3. `y = tree_min(z->right)` = `tree_min(g)`. Since `g->left == NULL`, `tree_min` returns `g` itself on its first check — no descent happened. `y == z->right`, i.e. `y->parent == z`. **This is the no-intermediate-parent case.**
4. `rb_free(z->key)` frees `"f"`'s string; `value_free(z->value)` frees `f`'s old value.
5. `z->key = y->key` ("g"); `z->value = y->value`. `f`'s node now holds `g`'s payload.
6. `n = y = g`; `free_own_payload = false`.
7. `child = (n->left) ? n->left : n->right` → `g->left == NULL` → `child = g->right = NULL`.
8. `n_was_black = is_black(g)` → `g` is red → `false`.
9. `transplant(t, g, NULL)` runs:
   - `v == NULL` → skip the `v->parent = u->parent` line (nothing to reparent).
   - `u->parent` is `f`, not `NULL` → go to the child-slot check.
   - `u == u->parent->left`? Is `g == f->left`? **No** — `f->left` is `e`. So the `else` branch fires: `u->parent->right = v` → **`f->right = NULL`**.

   Notice what just happened: the check and the write both used `u->parent` (== `z` == `f`) as *the* parent to fix up — the same field that would've been `p` in the deeper case. There's no branch anywhere in `transplant` that assumes `u->parent != z`; it just does the right thing because `y->parent` legitimately equals `z` here. No special case was needed, and none was written.
10. `n_was_black` is `false` → skip the recolor branch entirely (red-leaf removal, no debt).
11. `free_own_payload` is `false` → skip freeing `n->key`/`n->value` (they're `f`'s now).
12. `rb_free(n)` frees only `g`'s empty struct shell.
13. `t->size--`.

**After:**

```
                 f(B)          <- same struct, same color, same ->left
                /
             e(R)               <- untouched
```

...except this struct's `key`/`value` fields now read `"g"` and `g`'s old value. `f->right` is `NULL`. `f->parent`, `f->color`, and `f->left` were never written by any of this — only `f->right` and `f->key`/`f->value` changed, and only because `f` was `y`'s parent.

**Why it "just works":** `transplant` is driven entirely by `u->parent` (`y->parent`), never by an assumed distinct `p`. When `y->parent == z`, `u->parent` *is* `z`, so the same two lines (`u == u->parent->left` check, then the write) correctly patch `z`'s own child slot instead of some intermediate node's. This is the same reason CLRS's `y.parent == z` special case doesn't exist in our version at all — it was only ever needed there because CLRS physically relocates `y`'s node into `z`'s structural spot (reusing `z`'s old `left`/`right`/`color`), which creates a real ambiguity when `y` is that very child being overwritten. We never move `y`'s structural identity anywhere — we only ever touch `y`'s own parent slot, whatever it is.

Still no changes to `src/rbtree.c`.

message.content: show me how it works when the spliced node is the root

content.text:
Two sub-cases reach `n == t->root` (i.e. `n->parent == NULL`) — a bare single-node tree, and a root with exactly one child. Both go through the ≤1-child branch (`n == z`), never the two-children branch (there, `n` is always the successor `y`, somewhere in `z`'s right subtree, never `z`/root itself).

## Case 1: single-node tree (`"only"`, delete `"only"`)

```
Before:   root = only(B), no children
```

1. `z = find_node(t, "only")` → the root node.
2. `z->left == NULL && z->right == NULL` → two-children test fails → `n = z`.
3. `child = (n->left) ? n->left : n->right` → both `NULL` → `child = NULL`.
4. `n_was_black = is_black(n)` → `true` (root is always black).
5. `transplant(t, n, NULL)`:
   - `v == NULL` → skip `v->parent` assignment (nothing to reparent).
   - `u->parent == NULL`? **Yes** — `n` is the root → **`t->root = v = NULL`**.
6. `n_was_black && child != NULL`? `child` is `NULL` → skip the recolor branch entirely.
7. `free_own_payload` is `true` (no successor reduction happened) → `rb_free(n->key)`, `value_free(n->value)`.
8. `rb_free(n)`.
9. `t->size--` → `0`.

Result: `t->root == NULL`, `t->size == 0`. No fixup was needed or attempted — matches NOTES.md's own closing line: *"if the debt climbs all the way to the root: it just disappears."* Here it never even has to climb; there's no parent for a loop to run against in the first place.

## Case 2: root with one child (`"b","a"`, delete `"b"`)

```
Before:   b(B) root
          /
        a(R)
```

1. `z = find_node(t, "b")` → root.
2. Two-children test fails (`z->right == NULL`) → `n = z = b`.
3. `child = (n->left) ? n->left : n->right` → `n->left = a` → `child = a`.
4. `n_was_black = is_black(b)` → `true`.
5. `transplant(t, b, a)`:
   - `v = a`, non-NULL → **`a->parent = u->parent = b->parent = NULL`**.
   - `u->parent == NULL`? Yes → **`t->root = v = a`**.
6. `n_was_black && child != NULL` → both true → **`child->color = BLACK`** → `a` (the new root) is repainted black. This is the one-line STEP1 fixup, and it happens to simultaneously satisfy invariant 1 (root must be black) for the new root — not a coincidence, since a black node's only red child always becomes the correctly-colored replacement.

# rb_delete implementation plan (DRAFT — not yet approved)

Status: awaiting approval. Nothing in `src/rbtree.c` has been modified. `tests/test_rbtree.c`
already has the table-driven `rb_delete` tests from the prior session, but two of them need a
key-sequence correction noted below (also awaiting approval).

## Slice boundary

This slice implements **only**:
- STEP 0: two-children -> in-order-successor reduction (copy successor's key/value into the
  doomed node's slot, then delete the successor instead).
- STEP 1: splice a node with 0 or 1 children out of the tree, including the trivial "recolor
  the surviving red child black" case.

Explicitly **deferred** to a later, separately-approved slice:
- STEP 2: the doubly-black sibling/parent rebalancing loop (NOTES.md's "the real fixup loop"),
  and its mirror. Where it would be invoked, leave a comment marking the seam — not a stub
  function, not a partial implementation.

This boundary was chosen because 7 of our 9 table-driven test cases pass with only STEP 0+1
(verified by tracing each case against the actual insertion-fixup behavior, using an
instrumented scratch copy of rbtree.c to dump real colors — not by hand simulation alone,
which already produced one wrong conclusion during this planning pass). The 2 remaining cases
genuinely require STEP 2 and are expected to fail `rb_validate` until that slice lands.

## Private helpers needed

1. `static struct rb_node *find_node(const rbtree_t *t, const char *key)`
   BST search returning the node itself (not just its value, unlike `rb_find`). Needed because
   `rb_delete` must manipulate `parent`/`left`/`right`, not just read `value`. Small,
   unavoidable duplication of `rb_find`'s loop body.

2. `static struct rb_node *tree_min(struct rb_node *n)`
   Leftmost descendant of the subtree rooted at `n`. Gives the in-order successor as
   `tree_min(z->right)`.

3. `static void transplant(rbtree_t *t, struct rb_node *u, struct rb_node *v)`
   Puts `v` in `u`'s slot (inside `u->parent`, or `t->root` if `u` is the root), and sets
   `v->parent = u->parent` when `v != NULL`. The *only* place that touches `t->root` or
   reparents nodes during delete — mirrors how `rotate_left`/`rotate_right` already own that
   job for insert ("rotations own root maintenance", extended to transplant).

No `delete_fixup` helper this slice — deferred, will mirror `insert_fixup`'s
while-loop-with-mirror-branch shape when it's built.

## `rb_delete` body (pseudocode)

```c
int rb_delete(rbtree_t *t, const char *key) {
    struct rb_node *z = find_node(t, key);
    if (z == NULL) return -1;

    struct rb_node *n;              /* the node actually unlinked */
    bool free_own_payload = true;   /* does n still own the key/value to free? */

    if (z->left != NULL && z->right != NULL) {
        struct rb_node *y = tree_min(z->right);   /* in-order successor */
        rb_free(z->key);
        if (t->value_free) t->value_free(z->value);
        z->key   = y->key;      /* relocate y's payload into z's slot */
        z->value = y->value;
        n = y;
        free_own_payload = false;   /* n's key/value now belong to z */
    } else {
        n = z;
    }

    struct rb_node *child = (n->left != NULL) ? n->left : n->right; /* <=1 child, guaranteed */
    bool n_was_black = is_black(n);
    transplant(t, n, child);

    if (n_was_black) {
        if (child != NULL) child->color = BLACK; /* STEP1: absorbs the debt locally */
        /* else: doubly-black black-leaf case -- STEP2 loop, deferred */
    }

    if (free_own_payload) {
        rb_free(n->key);
        if (t->value_free) t->value_free(n->value);
    }
    rb_free(n);
    t->size--;
    return 0;
}
```

## Traced invariants (for defense / review)

- **Two children:** `z` is never physically removed. `y = tree_min(z->right)` is found,
  its key/value are relocated into `z` (after freeing `z`'s old key/value), then `y` itself
  is unlinked via the <=1-child path. `z` keeps its original color/position permanently.

- **Successor is `z`'s immediate right child (no intermediate parent):** `y == z->right`,
  so `y->parent == z`. `transplant(t, y, child)` is driven purely by `y->parent`, so it
  patches `z->right` directly with no special case — this is *why* the "copy payload, delete
  y in place" design (already committed to in NOTES.md) avoids CLRS's `y.parent == z` special
  case entirely: we never physically relocate `y`'s node into `z`'s structural spot the way
  CLRS's transplant-of-whole-nodes approach does.

- **Successor is deeper in the right subtree:** `y`'s real parent is some `p != z`, and
  `y == p->left` always (leftmost node). `y` may have a right child `r`. `transplant(t, y, r)`
  patches `p->left`; `z`'s own pointers (including `z->right`) are untouched.

- **Which physical node is unlinked:** always `n` -- either `z` (<=1 child) or `y` (two
  children). `z` is only ever physically removed when it had <=1 child to begin with.

  - Two-children case: `z`'s *old* key/value are freed **first**, immediately upon finding
    `y`, *before* any structural change. `y`'s own original key/value are **never freed by
    this call** -- they're relabeled as `z`'s. Only `y`'s empty struct is freed
    (`free_own_payload = false` guards this).
  - <=1-child case: `n == z`'s key/value are freed **after** the structural transplant,
    immediately before the struct itself is freed.
  - Aliasing window: from the moment of `z->key = y->key; z->value = y->value;` until
    `rb_free(n)` on `y`'s struct, both `z` and `y` hold identical pointer values for
    key/value. Harmless *as pointer values*; would be a use-after-free / double-free if
    anything ever called `rb_free`/`value_free` through `y`'s copy -- which is exactly what
    `free_own_payload` prevents.

  reparents nodes (same discipline as the rotations). `t->size--` happens exactly once, after
  the physical unlink, mirroring `rb_insert`'s single `t->size++`.

  root`); the two-children branch never produces `n == root` since `n` is always the
  successor there.
  - Single-node tree: `transplant(t, n, NULL)` sees `u->parent == NULL` -> `t->root = NULL`.
    No STEP1 recolor branch fires (`child == NULL`). Matches NOTES.md: "if the debt climbs
    all the way to the root: it just disappears" -- here it never even has to climb.
  - Root with one (necessarily red) child: `transplant(t, root, child)` sets
    `child->parent = NULL` and `t->root = child`; STEP1 then recolors `child` black,
    simultaneously restoring invariant 1 for the new root. No special-casing needed --
    `transplant`'s `u->parent == NULL` branch is the same one rotations already use.

## Table-driven test case audit (verified via instrumented scratch build, not hand simulation)

| case | structure found | outcome this slice |
|---|---|---|
| red leaf (`b,a,c`, delete `a`/`c`) | `b`(B) w/ `a`,`c`(R) leaves | passes |
| two children, root (`d,b,f,a,c,e,g`, delete `d`) | successor `e` is a red leaf | passes |
| two children, non-root (delete `f`) | successor `g` is a red leaf | passes |
| root, single node (delete `only`) | no parent, no loop needed regardless of color | passes |
| one red child, left (`b,a`, delete `b`) | `b`(B) root, `a`(R) child | passes |
| one red child, right (`a,b`, delete `a`) | mirror | passes |
| black leaf w/ red sibling (current test: `d,b,f,a,c`, delete `f`) | **mislabeled**: sibling `b` is BLACK w/ red children -> this is Case 4, not Case 5 | fails (needs STEP2 either way, but for the wrong stated reason) |
| mirror (current test: `d,f,b,e,g`, delete `b`) | same mislabeling, sibling `f` is BLACK | fails |

### Pending correction (needs sign-off before editing tests/test_rbtree.c)

Replace the two mislabeled cases with sequences verified (via instrumented scratch build) to
produce a genuinely RED immediate sibling:

- **Primary:** insert `c,b,d,f,g,l,n`; delete `b`. `b` is a black leaf, sibling `f` is RED
  (children `d` black-leaf, `l` black w/ red children `g`,`n`). Real Case 5
  (red sibling -> rotate+swap -> re-enter loop).
- **Mirror:** insert `p,n,l,k,c,i,e`; delete `p`. `p` is a black leaf, sibling `k` is RED on
  the *left*, forcing the mirrored rotation direction.

1. Approve or revise the pseudocode above.
2. Approve or revise the two corrected test sequences (edit to `tests/test_rbtree.c`).
3. Confirm slice boundary (stop before STEP2) is acceptable, i.e. it's fine for 2 of 9 table
   tests to remain red after this slice lands, pending the next slice.

  root`); the two-children branch never produces `n == root` since `n` is always the
  successor there.
  - Single-node tree: `transplant(t, n, NULL)` sees `u->parent == NULL` -> `t->root = NULL`.
    No STEP1 recolor branch fires (`child == NULL`). Matches NOTES.md: "if the debt climbs
    all the way to the root: it just disappears" -- here it never even has to climb.
  - Root with one (necessarily red) child: `transplant(t, root, child)` sets
    `child->parent = NULL` and `t->root = child`; STEP1 then recolors `child` black,
    simultaneously restoring invariant 1 for the new root. No special-casing needed --
    `transplant`'s `u->parent == NULL` branch is the same one rotations already use.

## The pending test-sequence correction

Two of the nine table-driven `rb_delete` tests are currently mislabeled. They're named "black leaf with red sibling" (and its mirror) — meant to exercise STEP 2's Case 5 (sibling is red → rotate it up over the parent, swap colors, then re-examine with the new sibling). But when I actually built the trees these insertion sequences produce (via an instrumented scratch copy of `rbtree.c` that dumps real node colors, not hand simulation — hand simulation had already led me to a wrong answer once), the sibling in both cases came out **black**, not red:

- `d,b,f,a,c` (delete `"f"`): `f`'s sibling is `b`, which is **black**, with two red children (`a`,`c`). That's Case 4, not Case 5.
- `d,f,b,e,g` (delete `"b"`): same mislabeling, mirrored.

Both cases still exercise *some* STEP 2 branch — so they're not useless — but they don't test what their names claim, and Case 4 vs. Case 5 are genuinely different code paths in the fixup loop. I searched (empirically, same scratch harness) for sequences that produce a real red immediate sibling and found:

- **Primary:** `c,b,d,f,g,l,n`, delete `b` → sibling `f` is genuinely red.
- **Mirror:** `p,n,l,k,c,i,e`, delete `p` → sibling `k` is genuinely red, on the left, forcing the mirrored rotation direction.

The correction is: replace the two mislabeled sequences in `tests/test_rbtree.c` with these. This is a test-file edit, so per NOTES.md's hard constraints ("never weaken, skip, or delete a test... if a test looks wrong, stop and explain why") I flagged it rather than silently fixing it.

## The three open items needing your approval

1. **The `rb_delete` pseudocode itself** — the two-children reduction via successor copy, the `transplant` helper, `find_node`/`tree_min`, and the STEP 1 recolor-only-if-one-red-child logic, all laid out in `PLAN.md`.
2. **The test-sequence correction above** — swapping in the two verified sequences.
3. **The slice boundary** — that it's acceptable for this round of work to leave those same two "red sibling" tests failing (correctly, on `rb_validate`, since STEP 2 isn't implemented yet), with the fixup loop deferred to a separately-approved follow-up slice.

Nothing's been written to `src/rbtree.c`. Say go and I'll start with slice 1+2 as scoped, or tell me what to change first.

content.text:
When `z`'s successor is `z->right` itself (i.e. `z->right->left == NULL`, so `tree_min` returns `z->right` immediately with no descent):

- `y = z->right`, so `y->parent == z` — there is no intermediate node `p` between them; `z` itself plays that role.
- `z`'s old key/value are freed, then overwritten with `y`'s (`z->key = y->key; z->value = y->value;`), same as any two-children case.
- `child = (y->left) ? y->left : y->right` → since `y->left == NULL`, `child = y->right` (call it `r`, which may itself be `NULL`).
- `transplant(t, y, r)` runs with `u->parent == z`: it sets `r->parent = z` (if `r` non-NULL) and, since `y == z->right` (not `z->left`), writes **`z->right = r`** directly — no special case, because the transplant logic is driven by `y->parent`, which just happens to equal `z` here.
- Everything else about `z` — its own `parent`, `color`, and `left` child — is untouched.
- `y`'s empty struct is freed (`free_own_payload = false`, so its stale key/value pointers, now aliased into `z`, are never touched).

Net effect: `z` keeps its position and color, gains `y`'s key/value, and its right subtree collapses from `y`'s old spot straight down to `r`. This is the exact scenario I traced concretely a couple turns ago using `d,b,f,a,c,e,g` (deleting `"f"`, successor `g`) — same mechanism, no extra code needed for it.

All three items are approved, so I'll proceed now: first fix the two mislabeled test sequences, then implement `rb_delete` per the approved pseudocode, then run `make test`/`asan`/`memcheck`.

1	# rb_delete implementation plan (DRAFT — not yet approved)
2	
3	Status: awaiting approval. Nothing in `src/rbtree.c` has been modified. `tests/test_rbtree.c`
4	already has the table-driven `rb_delete` tests from the prior session, but two of them need a
5	key-sequence correction noted below (also awaiting approval).
6	
7	## Slice boundary
8	
9	This slice implements **only**:
10	- STEP 0: two-children -> in-order-successor reduction (copy successor's key/value into the
11	  doomed node's slot, then delete the successor instead).
12	- STEP 1: splice a node with 0 or 1 children out of the tree, including the trivial "recolor
13	  the surviving red child black" case.
14	
15	Explicitly **deferred** to a later, separately-approved slice:
16	- STEP 2: the doubly-black sibling/parent rebalancing loop (NOTES.md's "the real fixup loop"),
17	  and its mirror. Where it would be invoked, leave a comment marking the seam — not a stub
18	  function, not a partial implementation.
19	
20	This boundary was chosen because 7 of our 9 table-driven test cases pass with only STEP 0+1
21	(verified by tracing each case against the actual insertion-fixup behavior, using an
22	instrumented scratch copy of rbtree.c to dump real colors — not by hand simulation alone,
23	which already produced one wrong conclusion during this planning pass). The 2 remaining cases
24	genuinely require STEP 2 and are expected to fail `rb_validate` until that slice lands.
25	
26	## Private helpers needed
27	
28	1. `static struct rb_node *find_node(const rbtree_t *t, const char *key)`
29	   BST search returning the node itself (not just its value, unlike `rb_find`). Needed because
30	   `rb_delete` must manipulate `parent`/`left`/`right`, not just read `value`. Small,
31	   unavoidable duplication of `rb_find`'s loop body.
32	
33	2. `static struct rb_node *tree_min(struct rb_node *n)`
34	   Leftmost descendant of the subtree rooted at `n`. Gives the in-order successor as
35	   `tree_min(z->right)`.
36	
37	3. `static void transplant(rbtree_t *t, struct rb_node *u, struct rb_node *v)`
38	   Puts `v` in `u`'s slot (inside `u->parent`, or `t->root` if `u` is the root), and sets
39	   `v->parent = u->parent` when `v != NULL`. The *only* place that touches `t->root` or
40	   reparents nodes during delete — mirrors how `rotate_left`/`rotate_right` already own that
41	   job for insert ("rotations own root maintenance", extended to transplant).
42	
43	No `delete_fixup` helper this slice — deferred, will mirror `insert_fixup`'s
44	while-loop-with-mirror-branch shape when it's built.
45	
46	## `rb_delete` body (pseudocode)
47	
48	```c
49	int rb_delete(rbtree_t *t, const char *key) {
50	    struct rb_node *z = find_node(t, key);
51	    if (z == NULL) return -1;
52	
53	    struct rb_node *n;              /* the node actually unlinked */
54	    bool free_own_payload = true;   /* does n still own the key/value to free? */
55	
56	    if (z->left != NULL && z->right != NULL) {
57	        struct rb_node *y = tree_min(z->right);   /* in-order successor */
58	        rb_free(z->key);
59	        if (t->value_free) t->value_free(z->value);
60	        z->key   = y->key;      /* relocate y's payload into z's slot */
61	        z->value = y->value;
62	        n = y;
63	        free_own_payload = false;   /* n's key/value now belong to z */
64	    } else {
65	        n = z;
66	    }
67	
68	    struct rb_node *child = (n->left != NULL) ? n->left : n->right; /* <=1 child, guaranteed */
69	    bool n_was_black = is_black(n);
70	    transplant(t, n, child);
71	
72	    if (n_was_black) {
73	        if (child != NULL) child->color = BLACK; /* STEP1: absorbs the debt locally */
74	        /* else: doubly-black black-leaf case -- STEP2 loop, deferred */
75	    }
76	
77	    if (free_own_payload) {
78	        rb_free(n->key);
79	        if (t->value_free) t->value_free(n->value);
80	    }
81	    rb_free(n);
82	    t->size--;
83	    return 0;
84	}
85	```
86	
87	## Traced invariants (for defense / review)
88	
89	- **Two children:** `z` is never physically removed. `y = tree_min(z->right)` is found,
90	  its key/value are relocated into `z` (after freeing `z`'s old key/value), then `y` itself
91	  is unlinked via the <=1-child path. `z` keeps its original color/position permanently.
92	
93	- **Successor is `z`'s immediate right child (no intermediate parent):** `y == z->right`,
94	  so `y->parent == z`. `transplant(t, y, child)` is driven purely by `y->parent`, so it
95	  patches `z->right` directly with no special case — this is *why* the "copy payload, delete
96	  y in place" design (already committed to in NOTES.md) avoids CLRS's `y.parent == z` special
97	  case entirely: we never physically relocate `y`'s node into `z`'s structural spot the way
98	  CLRS's transplant-of-whole-nodes approach does.
99	
100	- **Successor is deeper in the right subtree:** `y`'s real parent is some `p != z`, and
101	  `y == p->left` always (leftmost node). `y` may have a right child `r`. `transplant(t, y, r)`
102	  patches `p->left`; `z`'s own pointers (including `z->right`) are untouched.
103	
104	- **Which physical node is unlinked:** always `n` -- either `z` (<=1 child) or `y` (two
105	  children). `z` is only ever physically removed when it had <=1 child to begin with.
106	
107	- **Key/value ownership timeline (two distinct free call-sites, not one):**
108	  - Two-children case: `z`'s *old* key/value are freed **first**, immediately upon finding
109	    `y`, *before* any structural change. `y`'s own original key/value are **never freed by
110	    this call** -- they're relabeled as `z`'s. Only `y`'s empty struct is freed
111	    (`free_own_payload = false` guards this).
112	  - <=1-child case: `n == z`'s key/value are freed **after** the structural transplant,
113	    immediately before the struct itself is freed.
114	  - Aliasing window: from the moment of `z->key = y->key; z->value = y->value;` until
115	    `rb_free(n)` on `y`'s struct, both `z` and `y` hold identical pointer values for
116	    key/value. Harmless *as pointer values*; would be a use-after-free / double-free if
117	    anything ever called `rb_free`/`value_free` through `y`'s copy -- which is exactly what
118	    `free_own_payload` prevents.
119	
120	- **`t->root` / parent pointers / `t->size`:** only `transplant` touches `t->root` or
121	  reparents nodes (same discipline as the rotations). `t->size--` happens exactly once, after
122	  the physical unlink, mirroring `rb_insert`'s single `t->size++`.
123	
124	- **Spliced node is the root:** two sub-cases, both via the <=1-child branch (`n == z ==
125	  root`); the two-children branch never produces `n == root` since `n` is always the
126	  successor there.
127	  - Single-node tree: `transplant(t, n, NULL)` sees `u->parent == NULL` -> `t->root = NULL`.
128	    No STEP1 recolor branch fires (`child == NULL`). Matches NOTES.md: "if the debt climbs
129	    all the way to the root: it just disappears" -- here it never even has to climb.
130	  - Root with one (necessarily red) child: `transplant(t, root, child)` sets
131	    `child->parent = NULL` and `t->root = child`; STEP1 then recolors `child` black,
132	    simultaneously restoring invariant 1 for the new root. No special-casing needed --
133	    `transplant`'s `u->parent == NULL` branch is the same one rotations already use.
134	
135	## Table-driven test case audit (verified via instrumented scratch build, not hand simulation)
136	
137	| case | structure found | outcome this slice |
138	|---|---|---|
139	| red leaf (`b,a,c`, delete `a`/`c`) | `b`(B) w/ `a`,`c`(R) leaves | passes |
140	| two children, root (`d,b,f,a,c,e,g`, delete `d`) | successor `e` is a red leaf | passes |
141	| two children, non-root (delete `f`) | successor `g` is a red leaf | passes |
142	| root, single node (delete `only`) | no parent, no loop needed regardless of color | passes |
143	| one red child, left (`b,a`, delete `b`) | `b`(B) root, `a`(R) child | passes |
144	| one red child, right (`a,b`, delete `a`) | mirror | passes |
145	| black leaf w/ red sibling (current test: `d,b,f,a,c`, delete `f`) | **mislabeled**: sibling `b` is BLACK w/ red children -> this is Case 4, not Case 5 | fails (needs STEP2 either way, but for the wrong stated reason) |
146	| mirror (current test: `d,f,b,e,g`, delete `b`) | same mislabeling, sibling `f` is BLACK | fails |
147	
148	### Pending correction (needs sign-off before editing tests/test_rbtree.c)
149	
150	Replace the two mislabeled cases with sequences verified (via instrumented scratch build) to
151	produce a genuinely RED immediate sibling:
152	
153	- **Primary:** insert `c,b,d,f,g,l,n`; delete `b`. `b` is a black leaf, sibling `f` is RED
154	  (children `d` black-leaf, `l` black w/ red children `g`,`n`). Real Case 5
155	  (red sibling -> rotate+swap -> re-enter loop).
156	- **Mirror:** insert `p,n,l,k,c,i,e`; delete `p`. `p` is a black leaf, sibling `k` is RED on
157	  the *left*, forcing the mirrored rotation direction.
158	
159	## Open items before implementation begins

# rb_delete implementation plan (DRAFT — not yet approved)

Status: awaiting approval. Nothing in `src/rbtree.c` has been modified. `tests/test_rbtree.c`
already has the table-driven `rb_delete` tests from the prior session, but two of them need a
key-sequence correction noted below (also awaiting approval).

## Slice boundary

This slice implements **only**:
- STEP 0: two-children -> in-order-successor reduction (copy successor's key/value into the
  doomed node's slot, then delete the successor instead).
- STEP 1: splice a node with 0 or 1 children out of the tree, including the trivial "recolor
  the surviving red child black" case.

Explicitly **deferred** to a later, separately-approved slice:
- STEP 2: the doubly-black sibling/parent rebalancing loop (NOTES.md's "the real fixup loop"),
  and its mirror. Where it would be invoked, leave a comment marking the seam — not a stub
  function, not a partial implementation.

This boundary was chosen because 7 of our 9 table-driven test cases pass with only STEP 0+1
(verified by tracing each case against the actual insertion-fixup behavior, using an
instrumented scratch copy of rbtree.c to dump real colors — not by hand simulation alone,
which already produced one wrong conclusion during this planning pass). The 2 remaining cases
genuinely require STEP 2 and are expected to fail `rb_validate` until that slice lands.

## Private helpers needed

1. `static struct rb_node *find_node(const rbtree_t *t, const char *key)`
   BST search returning the node itself (not just its value, unlike `rb_find`). Needed because
   `rb_delete` must manipulate `parent`/`left`/`right`, not just read `value`. Small,
   unavoidable duplication of `rb_find`'s loop body.

2. `static struct rb_node *tree_min(struct rb_node *n)`
   Leftmost descendant of the subtree rooted at `n`. Gives the in-order successor as
   `tree_min(z->right)`.

3. `static void transplant(rbtree_t *t, struct rb_node *u, struct rb_node *v)`
   Puts `v` in `u`'s slot (inside `u->parent`, or `t->root` if `u` is the root), and sets
   `v->parent = u->parent` when `v != NULL`. The *only* place that touches `t->root` or
   reparents nodes during delete — mirrors how `rotate_left`/`rotate_right` already own that
   job for insert ("rotations own root maintenance", extended to transplant).

No `delete_fixup` helper this slice — deferred, will mirror `insert_fixup`'s
while-loop-with-mirror-branch shape when it's built.

## `rb_delete` body (pseudocode)

```c
int rb_delete(rbtree_t *t, const char *key) {
    struct rb_node *z = find_node(t, key);
    if (z == NULL) return -1;

    struct rb_node *n;              /* the node actually unlinked */
    bool free_own_payload = true;   /* does n still own the key/value to free? */

    if (z->left != NULL && z->right != NULL) {
        struct rb_node *y = tree_min(z->right);   /* in-order successor */
        rb_free(z->key);
        if (t->value_free) t->value_free(z->value);
        z->key   = y->key;      /* relocate y's payload into z's slot */
        z->value = y->value;
        n = y;
        free_own_payload = false;   /* n's key/value now belong to z */
    } else {
        n = z;
    }

    struct rb_node *child = (n->left != NULL) ? n->left : n->right; /* <=1 child, guaranteed */
    bool n_was_black = is_black(n);
    transplant(t, n, child);

    if (n_was_black) {
        if (child != NULL) child->color = BLACK; /* STEP1: absorbs the debt locally */
        /* else: doubly-black black-leaf case -- STEP2 loop, deferred */
    }

    if (free_own_payload) {
        rb_free(n->key);
        if (t->value_free) t->value_free(n->value);
    }
    rb_free(n);
    t->size--;
    return 0;
}
```

## Traced invariants (for defense / review)

- **Two children:** `z` is never physically removed. `y = tree_min(z->right)` is found,
  its key/value are relocated into `z` (after freeing `z`'s old key/value), then `y` itself
  is unlinked via the <=1-child path. `z` keeps its original color/position permanently.

- **Successor is `z`'s immediate right child (no intermediate parent):** `y == z->right`,
  so `y->parent == z`. `transplant(t, y, child)` is driven purely by `y->parent`, so it
  patches `z->right` directly with no special case — this is *why* the "copy payload, delete
  y in place" design (already committed to in NOTES.md) avoids CLRS's `y.parent == z` special
  case entirely: we never physically relocate `y`'s node into `z`'s structural spot the way
  CLRS's transplant-of-whole-nodes approach does.

- **Successor is deeper in the right subtree:** `y`'s real parent is some `p != z`, and
  `y == p->left` always (leftmost node). `y` may have a right child `r`. `transplant(t, y, r)`
  patches `p->left`; `z`'s own pointers (including `z->right`) are untouched.

- **Which physical node is unlinked:** always `n` -- either `z` (<=1 child) or `y` (two
  children). `z` is only ever physically removed when it had <=1 child to begin with.

- **Key/value ownership timeline (two distinct free call-sites, not one):**
  - Two-children case: `z`'s *old* key/value are freed **first**, immediately upon finding
    `y`, *before* any structural change. `y`'s own original key/value are **never freed by
    this call** -- they're relabeled as `z`'s. Only `y`'s empty struct is freed
    (`free_own_payload = false` guards this).
  - <=1-child case: `n == z`'s key/value are freed **after** the structural transplant,
    immediately before the struct itself is freed.
  - Aliasing window: from the moment of `z->key = y->key; z->value = y->value;` until
    `rb_free(n)` on `y`'s struct, both `z` and `y` hold identical pointer values for
    key/value. Harmless *as pointer values*; would be a use-after-free / double-free if
    anything ever called `rb_free`/`value_free` through `y`'s copy -- which is exactly what
    `free_own_payload` prevents.

- **`t->root` / parent pointers / `t->size`:** only `transplant` touches `t->root` or
  reparents nodes (same discipline as the rotations). `t->size--` happens exactly once, after
  the physical unlink, mirroring `rb_insert`'s single `t->size++`.

- **Spliced node is the root:** two sub-cases, both via the <=1-child branch (`n == z ==
  root`); the two-children branch never produces `n == root` since `n` is always the
  successor there.
  - Single-node tree: `transplant(t, n, NULL)` sees `u->parent == NULL` -> `t->root = NULL`.
    No STEP1 recolor branch fires (`child == NULL`). Matches NOTES.md: "if the debt climbs
    all the way to the root: it just disappears" -- here it never even has to climb.
  - Root with one (necessarily red) child: `transplant(t, root, child)` sets
    `child->parent = NULL` and `t->root = child`; STEP1 then recolors `child` black,
    simultaneously restoring invariant 1 for the new root. No special-casing needed --
    `transplant`'s `u->parent == NULL` branch is the same one rotations already use.

## Table-driven test case audit (verified via instrumented scratch build, not hand simulation)

| case | structure found | outcome this slice |
|---|---|---|
| red leaf (`b,a,c`, delete `a`/`c`) | `b`(B) w/ `a`,`c`(R) leaves | passes |
| two children, root (`d,b,f,a,c,e,g`, delete `d`) | successor `e` is a red leaf | passes |
| two children, non-root (delete `f`) | successor `g` is a red leaf | passes |
| root, single node (delete `only`) | no parent, no loop needed regardless of color | passes |
| one red child, left (`b,a`, delete `b`) | `b`(B) root, `a`(R) child | passes |
| one red child, right (`a,b`, delete `a`) | mirror | passes |
| black leaf w/ red sibling (current test: `d,b,f,a,c`, delete `f`) | **mislabeled**: sibling `b` is BLACK w/ red children -> this is Case 4, not Case 5 | fails (needs STEP2 either way, but for the wrong stated reason) |
| mirror (current test: `d,f,b,e,g`, delete `b`) | same mislabeling, sibling `f` is BLACK | fails |

### Pending correction (needs sign-off before editing tests/test_rbtree.c)

Replace the two mislabeled cases with sequences verified (via instrumented scratch build) to
produce a genuinely RED immediate sibling:

- **Primary:** insert `c,b,d,f,g,l,n`; delete `b`. `b` is a black leaf, sibling `f` is RED
  (children `d` black-leaf, `l` black w/ red children `g`,`n`). Real Case 5
  (red sibling -> rotate+swap -> re-enter loop).
- **Mirror:** insert `p,n,l,k,c,i,e`; delete `p`. `p` is a black leaf, sibling `k` is RED on
  the *left*, forcing the mirrored rotation direction.

## Open items before implementation begins

1. Approve or revise the pseudocode above.
2. Approve or revise the two corrected test sequences (edit to `tests/test_rbtree.c`).
3. Confirm slice boundary (stop before STEP2) is acceptable, i.e. it's fine for 2 of 9 table
   tests to remain red after this slice lands, pending the next slice.

I read `src/rbtree.c` (rotations at 51–73, `insert_fixup` at 75–118, `transplant` at 177–182, `rb_delete` at 184–220) and the NOTES.md deletion-case devlog. Verdicts below.

## 1. Is the mirror exact/correct?

**Correct.** I checked it structurally and then empirically via a full hand-trace (Q5 below), which came out as the exact mirror shape of the primary-branch trace — a sign error would have shown up as an asymmetric result.

Point-by-point mapping (primary → mirror):
- `sib = parent->right` → `sib = parent->left` ✓
- Case 5: `rotate_left(t, parent)` → `rotate_right(t, parent)`, re-fetch matches new side ✓
- Case 3 (`is_black(sib->left) && is_black(sib->right)`): identical in both branches — correctly *not* mirrored, since this check has no side-dependence ✓
- Far-nephew check: primary tests `sib->right` (far side for a left‑hand `x`), mirror tests `sib->left` (far side for a right‑hand `x`) — correct, this is the one detail people usually get backwards ✓
- Near-rotate: primary paints `sib->left` black then `rotate_right(t, sib)`; mirror paints `sib->right` black then `rotate_left(t, sib)` — correctly swapped ✓
- Terminal Case 4: primary finishes with `sib->right` painted black + `rotate_left(t, parent)`; mirror finishes with `sib->left` painted black + `rotate_right(t, parent)` — correctly swapped ✓

No copy-paste sign errors found.

## 2. Can `sib` be NULL when dereferenced?

**No, and the code is right not to guard it.** Standard RB argument: when `delete_fixup` is entered/re-entered, `x`'s side is "doubly black" — it must contribute one *more* black node than it actually has. Since even `x == NULL` counts 1 toward black-height, the required count on `x`'s side is ≥2, and by invariant 3 that equals the real black-height on `sib`'s side. So `sib`'s subtree must have black-height ≥2, which is impossible for `sib == NULL` (bh 1). Hence `sib` is always non-NULL, both on entry and immediately after the Case‑5 rotation (`sib`'s pre-rotation self was RED and contributed 0, so *both* of its children individually needed black-height 2 — neither can be NULL). `sib->left`/`sib->right` themselves are correctly *not* assumed non-NULL — every dereference of *their* `->color` is properly guarded (`if (sib->left != NULL) ...`), even though in the specific branches reached those guards are provably dead code (e.g. in the near-rotate step, `sib->left` is known RED, hence non-NULL, by construction of the `else` branch). That redundancy is harmless defensive style, not a bug.

## 3. Termination

**Terminates, no infinite-loop risk.**
- Case 5 does not re-enter the `while`; it falls through into the same iteration's Case 3/4 check (matches CLRS's structure, not a bug).
- Case 4 always `return`s — ends the function outright.
- Case 3 is the only path that continues the `while`: it strictly increases `parent`'s height (equivalently strictly decreases `x`'s depth by exactly 1), bounded below by the root (`parent == NULL` stops it) or by `x` turning RED (loop guard `is_black(x)` stops it). Depth is a finite non-negative integer, so at most O(h) iterations, mirroring `insert_fixup`'s termination argument.

## 4. Is capturing `parent = n->parent` *after* `transplant` actually the load-bearing detail?

**Safe, but the stated rationale slightly misattributes why.** `transplant` never writes `u->parent` (only `v->parent` and `u->parent`'s child-slot). So `n->parent`'s *value* is identical whether read before or after the `transplant` call — capturing it "after" buys nothing by itself. What actually matters, and what the code gets right, is that **the call to `delete_fixup` itself must happen after `transplant` has run**, because `delete_fixup`'s very first comparison (`x == parent->left`) depends on `parent->left`/`parent->right` already holding `child` (NULL) in `n`'s old slot — and that side-effect is what `transplant` performs. The code does sequence it correctly (`transplant(...)` at line 205, then the `delete_fixup` call afterward), so there's no bug — just a documentation nit: the safety comment should say "safe because `transplant` already ran before this call, not specifically because we read `n->parent` after `transplant`."

## 5. Hand traces

**Trace 1 (delete "b"):** PASS. `parent=c, x=NULL`. `x==parent->left` (NULL==NULL) → primary branch. `sib=f` is RED → Case 5: `f=BLACK, c=RED`, `rotate_left(t,c)`, new `sib=d`. `d`'s children both NULL/black → Case 3: `d=RED`, `x=c`, `parent=c->parent=f`. Loop re-check: `is_black(x=c)` is false (c is RED from Case 5) → loop exits. Final: `c->color=BLACK`.

Final shape:
```
        f(BLACK)
       /        \
     c(BLACK)    l(BLACK)
     /    \       /    \
   NULL  d(RED) g(RED) n(RED)
```
Black-height from f is uniformly 2 on every path — consistent, matches pre-deletion height as seen from above `c`'s old position. This is the textbook Case 5 → Case 3 sequence.

**Trace 2 (delete "p"):** The tree *as literally stated has an invariant-2 violation before deletion even starts*: `k` is RED and one of its children `i` is also stated RED — a red node cannot have a red child. This can't be a valid pre-deletion RBT, so I flag it as an error in the given fixture (line: "k's children are i(RED) and e(BLACK)"). Assuming the obvious correction that mirrors trace 1 (`i` must be BLACK, a leaf, playing `d`'s role; `e`, playing `l`'s role, is `k`'s far/left child), the trace becomes:

`parent=n_node, x=NULL`. `x==parent->left`? No — `x` is NULL but `parent->left` is `k`, so it's not the primary ("x==parent->left") match; falls to the `else` (mirror) branch, correctly identifying the deficient side as right. `sib=k` is RED → Case 5 mirror: `k=BLACK, n_node=RED`, `rotate_right(t, n_node)`, new `sib=n_node->left=i`. `i`'s children both black/NULL → Case 3: `i=RED`, `x=n_node`, `parent=n_node->parent=k`. `is_black(x=n_node)` false (RED from Case 5) → exit loop → `n_node->color=BLACK`.

Final shape:
```
            k(BLACK)
           /        \
        e(BLACK)   n_node(BLACK)
        /              /    \
   c_node(RED)      i(RED)  NULL
```
This is the exact mirror image of Trace 1's result (`k`↔`f`, `e`↔`l`, `n_node`↔`c`, `i`↔`d`). **PASS**, modulo the input typo noted above, which should be fixed in the test fixture/quiz material before using it, since as written it's not a legal starting tree.

## 6. Other issues

None found beyond the fixture typo in Trace 2. Specifically checked and confirmed fine:
- Root-deletion edge case (single-node tree, delete the black-leaf root): `delete_fixup(t, NULL, NULL)` — loop body never runs, no recolor, correctly matches "debt climbs to the root and disappears."
- STEP 1's red-child splice (existing lines 207–209) is correctly *not* routed through `delete_fixup` at all — matches NOTES.md's explicit "Case 6, no sibling-fixup should run."
- Color-then-rotate ordering within the near-rotation and terminal steps is irrelevant to correctness since rotations here are pure structural rewires and don't touch color fields — no ordering bug.
- No use-after-free: `n` isn't freed until after `delete_fixup` returns, and `delete_fixup` never touches `n` itself, only `parent`/`x`/`sib` derived from already-live nodes.

## Summary

The design is correct as specified: exact mirror, safe dereferencing (justified by the standard black-height argument, not just asserted), provable termination, and the `transplant`-then-`delete_fixup` ordering is safe (though the write-up's "read after transplant" framing should be tightened to "call after transplant").   so `y->parent == z`. `transplant(t, y, child)` is driven purely by `y->parent`, so it
  patches `z->right` directly with no special case — this is *why* the "copy payload, delete
  y in place" design (already committed to in NOTES.md) avoids CLRS's `y.parent == z` special
  case entirely: we never physically relocate `y`'s node into `z`'s structural spot the way
  CLRS's transplant-of-whole-nodes approach does.

- **Successor is deeper in the right subtree:** `y`'s real parent is some `p != z`, and
  `y == p->left` always (leftmost node). `y` may have a right child `r`. `transplant(t, y, r)`
  patches `p->left`; `z`'s own pointers (including `z->right`) are untouched.

- **Which physical node is unlinked:** always `n` -- either `z` (<=1 child) or `y` (two
  children). `z` is only ever physically removed when it had <=1 child to begin with.

- **Key/value ownership timeline (two distinct free call-sites, not one):**
  - Two-children case: `z`'s *old* key/value are freed **first**, immediately upon finding
    `y`, *before* any structural change. `y`'s own original key/value are **never freed by
    this call** -- they're relabeled as `z`'s. Only `y`'s empty struct is freed
    (`free_own_payload = false` guards this).
  - <=1-child case: `n == z`'s key/value are freed **after** the structural transplant,
    immediately before the struct itself is freed.
  - Aliasing window: from the moment of `z->key = y->key; z->value = y->value;` until
    `rb_free(n)` on `y`'s struct, both `z` and `y` hold identical pointer values for
    key/value. Harmless *as pointer values*; would be a use-after-free / double-free if
    anything ever called `rb_free`/`value_free` through `y`'s copy -- which is exactly what
    `free_own_payload` prevents.

- **`t->root` / parent pointers / `t->size`:** only `transplant` touches `t->root` or
  reparents nodes (same discipline as the rotations). `t->size--` happens exactly once, after
  the physical unlink, mirroring `rb_insert`'s single `t->size++`.

- **Spliced node is the root:** two sub-cases, both via the <=1-child branch (`n == z ==
  root`); the two-children branch never produces `n == root` since `n` is always the
  successor there.
  - Single-node tree: `transplant(t, n, NULL)` sees `u->parent == NULL` -> `t->root = NULL`.
    No STEP1 recolor branch fires (`child == NULL`). Matches NOTES.md: "if the debt climbs
    all the way to the root: it just disappears" -- here it never even has to climb.
  - Root with one (necessarily red) child: `transplant(t, root, child)` sets
    `child->parent = NULL` and `t->root = child`; STEP1 then recolors `child` black,
    simultaneously restoring invariant 1 for the new root. No special-casing needed --
    `transplant`'s `u->parent == NULL` branch is the same one rotations already use.

entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

content.text:
I re-verified all 9 cases from scratch — not just re-running the existing tests, but rebuilding an instrumented scratch copy of `rbtree.c` that dumps real node colors/structure before and after each delete, so I can confirm each case actually exercises the code path its name claims (the same method that caught the earlier mislabeling bug).

**Findings: no discrepancies.** Every case matches its intended path exactly:

| case | pre-delete target | path taken | post-delete |
|---|---|---|---|
| red leaf / mirror | RED leaf | STEP1 red-leaf, no fixup | validate=0 |
| **black leaf w/ red sibling** | `b`: BLACK leaf, sibling `f` RED | **Case 5 → Case 3**, `delete_fixup` fires | validate=0 |
| **mirror** | `p`: BLACK leaf, sibling `k` RED (left) | **Case 5 mirror → Case 3 mirror** | validate=0 |
| two children (root/non-root) | successor is a RED leaf both times | reduces to red-leaf removal, `delete_fixup` never called | validate=0 |
| root, single node | root, no parent | `delete_fixup(t, NULL, NULL)` — loop never runs | validate=0 |
| one red child (both) | BLACK w/ 1 RED child | STEP1 trivial recolor, no loop | validate=0 |

The two cases that actually exercise `delete_fixup` (rows 2–3) are the ones worth double-checking hardest, since that's the newest, riskiest code. I hand-verified their post-delete structures against the dump:

- **Primary** (`c,b,d,f,g,l,n`, delete `b`): `f` (red sibling) rotates up over `c`, colors swap; new sibling `d` (black leaf) triggers Case 3 recolor; climbs to `c`, which was just reddened by the swap, so the loop exits and `c` is forced black. Final: `f`(B) root, `f→left = c`(B)`[NULL, d(R)]`, `f→right = l`(B)`[g(R), n(R)]` — matches the black-height math by hand (every path from `f` carries exactly 2 blacks).

# Extend tests/fuzz.c to exercise rb_delete

## Context

`rb_delete` is now fully implemented (STEP0 successor-reduction, STEP1 splice, STEP2
`delete_fixup` loop + mirror -- committed `8fa9072`). The 9 hand-built table-driven cases in
`tests/test_rbtree.c` each pin down one specific, chosen-by-hand structural scenario (red leaf,
black leaf w/ red sibling, two children, etc.). What they *can't* exercise is a multi-level
`delete_fixup` climb (Case 3 recoloring and moving up more than one ancestor) or a debt that
climbs all the way to the actual tree root -- those only show up in trees deep/varied enough
that nobody would hand-construct them. That's exactly the gap the spec's fuzzer requirement is
for: `NOTES.md`'s Thresholds section requires the fuzzer to run >= 10^5 random
**insert/find/delete** operations against a reference model, calling `rb_validate` at least
every 100 ops, clean under both asan and memcheck. `tests/fuzz.c` currently only does
insert/find. This plan closes that gap.

## How the existing fuzz.c works (for your walkthrough)

Read top to bottom, `tests/fuzz.c` is:

1. **A reference-model oracle** (lines ~10-60): `struct model` is a flat, unsorted array of
   `{key, value}` pairs -- not a tree, not sorted, just a linear list kept deliberately dumb so
   it's obviously correct and can't share a bug with `rbtree.c`. `model_find` does a linear
   scan (`strcmp` against every entry) -- O(n), but this is a correctness oracle, not something
   that needs to be fast. `model_put` either overwrites an existing entry's value (freeing the
   old one first -- mirrors the tree's own overwrite contract) or grows the array (doubling
   capacity, like a typical dynamic array) and appends. `model_destroy` frees everything.

2. **A random key generator** (`make_key`, ~line 62): produces strings like `"key002381"` drawn
   from a fixed-size key space (`key_space = 5000`) via `rand() % key_space`. Because the space
   is much smaller than the op count, keys collide constantly on purpose -- that's what
   produces overwrites, repeated deletes of the same already-gone key, etc.

3. **The main loop** (~line 80 onward), one iteration per op:
   - Pick a random key.
   - Coin-flip (`rand() % 2`) between insert and find.
   - **Insert branch**: allocate a value, call `rb_insert`, check the return code, immediately
     `rb_find` it back to confirm the tree can find what it just stored, then `model_put` to
     keep the oracle in sync.
   - **Find branch**: look the key up in *both* the model and the tree, and require they agree
     -- either both say "absent", or both return the same value pointer.
   - Every 100 ops, call `rb_validate` and bail loudly (`fprintf(stderr, ...); return 1;`) if any
     invariant breaks, printing which one (`rb_validate`'s return code names the violated
     invariant).
   - After every op, assert `rb_size(t) == m.count` -- the model's count is the ground truth for
     "how many entries should exist," so this catches any op that silently drops or duplicates
     a node.
   - After the loop: one final `rb_validate`, then tear down both the tree and the model.

The whole design's point is: **the model can never be wrong** (it's too simple to have the same
bugs as the tree), so any disagreement between tree and model, or any invariant violation, is
unambiguously a real bug in `rbtree.c`.

## The extension

Minimal, same-pattern addition -- no new files, no new structures beyond one helper:

1. **`model_delete(struct model *m, const char *key)`** (new function, next to `model_put`):
   linear-scan for the entry, `free` its key and value, then compact by swapping the last
   entry into the freed slot and decrementing `count`. Order doesn't matter (the model was
   never sorted), so this is the simplest correct removal -- O(1) once found, no shifting.

2. **Widen the op choice from 2-way to 3-way**: `rand() % 2` becomes `rand() % 3` (insert / find
   / delete), same style as the existing coin-flip, just one more branch.

3. **Delete branch** (new, parallel structure to the existing find branch):
   ```c
   struct model_entry *e = model_find(&m, keybuf);
   int rc = rb_delete(t, keybuf);
   if (e == NULL) {
       if (rc != -1) { /* fprintf + return 1: rb_delete succeeded on an absent key */ }
   } else {
       if (rc != 0) { /* fprintf + return 1: rb_delete failed on a key that exists */ }
       model_delete(&m, keybuf);
       if (rb_find(t, keybuf) != NULL) { /* fprintf + return 1: key still findable post-delete */ }
   }
   ```
   This checks both directions of the contract (spec's ownership section, and
   `include/rbtree.h`'s comment on `rb_delete`): absent key -> `-1`, tree unchanged; present key
   -> `0`, and the key is now genuinely gone from the tree, not just from the model.

4. **Everything else is untouched and just starts covering delete for free**: the periodic
   `rb_validate` (now also catching any `delete_fixup` black-height regression), and the
   post-op `rb_size(t) == m.count` check (now also catching an off-by-one from a botched
   splice or a missed `t->size--`), already run unconditionally every iteration regardless of
   which branch fired.

No changes anywhere in `src/rbtree.c` -- this is purely a test-harness change.

## Why this specifically closes last turn's flagged gap

With inserts and deletes both drawn from the same 5000-key space over 100k+ ops, the tree will
naturally grow, shrink, and get restructured through long chains of rotations from both
`insert_fixup` and `delete_fixup` -- producing exactly the deep, multi-level `delete_fixup`
Case-3 climbs (and eventually a climb that reaches the actual root) that the 9 hand-picked
table cases can't reach by construction. Any bug there surfaces either as an `rb_validate`
failure (invariant 3, black-height) within 100 ops of when it happened, or as a
tree/model/size disagreement immediately.

## Verification

1. `make test` -- now runs `./build/fuzz 100000` doing a real mix of insert/find/delete;
   expect `fuzz: 100000 insert/find/delete ops OK` (update the success message to say
   "insert/find/delete" instead of "insert/find").
2. `make asan` -- same run under ASan/UBSan.
3. `make memcheck` -- valgrind run at the existing lower op count (20000, already set in the
   Makefile for speed under valgrind's overhead).
4. Re-run a few times with different seeds (the fuzzer already accepts an optional seed as
   `argv[2]`) to get variety across runs, same as it already supports today.

# Extend tests/fuzz.c to exercise rb_delete

## Context

`rb_delete` is now fully implemented (STEP0 successor-reduction, STEP1 splice, STEP2
`delete_fixup` loop + mirror -- committed `8fa9072`). The 9 hand-built table-driven cases in
`tests/test_rbtree.c` each pin down one specific, chosen-by-hand structural scenario (red leaf,
black leaf w/ red sibling, two children, etc.). What they *can't* exercise is a multi-level
`delete_fixup` climb (Case 3 recoloring and moving up more than one ancestor) or a debt that
climbs all the way to the actual tree root -- those only show up in trees deep/varied enough
that nobody would hand-construct them. That's exactly the gap the spec's fuzzer requirement is
for: `NOTES.md`'s Thresholds section requires the fuzzer to run >= 10^5 random
**insert/find/delete** operations against a reference model, calling `rb_validate` at least
every 100 ops, clean under both asan and memcheck. `tests/fuzz.c` currently only does
insert/find. This plan closes that gap.

## How the existing fuzz.c works (for your walkthrough)

Read top to bottom, `tests/fuzz.c` is:

1. **A reference-model oracle** (lines ~10-60): `struct model` is a flat, unsorted array of
   `{key, value}` pairs -- not a tree, not sorted, just a linear list kept deliberately dumb so
   it's obviously correct and can't share a bug with `rbtree.c`. `model_find` does a linear
   scan (`strcmp` against every entry) -- O(n), but this is a correctness oracle, not something
   that needs to be fast. `model_put` either overwrites an existing entry's value (freeing the
   old one first -- mirrors the tree's own overwrite contract) or grows the array (doubling
   capacity, like a typical dynamic array) and appends. `model_destroy` frees everything.

2. **A random key generator** (`make_key`, ~line 62): produces strings like `"key002381"` drawn
   from a fixed-size key space (`key_space = 5000`) via `rand() % key_space`. Because the space
   is much smaller than the op count, keys collide constantly on purpose -- that's what
   produces overwrites, repeated deletes of the same already-gone key, etc.

3. **The main loop** (~line 80 onward), one iteration per op:
   - Pick a random key.
   - Coin-flip (`rand() % 2`) between insert and find.
   - **Insert branch**: allocate a value, call `rb_insert`, check the return code, immediately
     `rb_find` it back to confirm the tree can find what it just stored, then `model_put` to
     keep the oracle in sync.
   - **Find branch**: look the key up in *both* the model and the tree, and require they agree
     -- either both say "absent", or both return the same value pointer.
   - Every 100 ops, call `rb_validate` and bail loudly (`fprintf(stderr, ...); return 1;`) if any
     invariant breaks, printing which one (`rb_validate`'s return code names the violated
     invariant).
   - After every op, assert `rb_size(t) == m.count` -- the model's count is the ground truth for
     "how many entries should exist," so this catches any op that silently drops or duplicates
     a node.
   - After the loop: one final `rb_validate`, then tear down both the tree and the model.

The whole design's point is: **the model can never be wrong** (it's too simple to have the same
bugs as the tree), so any disagreement between tree and model, or any invariant violation, is
unambiguously a real bug in `rbtree.c`.

## The extension

Minimal, same-pattern addition -- no new files, no new structures beyond one helper:

1. **`model_delete(struct model *m, const char *key)`** (new function, next to `model_put`):
   linear-scan for the entry, `free` its key and value, then compact by swapping the last
   entry into the freed slot and decrementing `count`. Order doesn't matter (the model was
   never sorted), so this is the simplest correct removal -- O(1) once found, no shifting.

2. **Widen the op choice from 2-way to 3-way**: `rand() % 2` becomes `rand() % 3` (insert / find
   / delete), same style as the existing coin-flip, just one more branch.

3. **Delete branch** (new, parallel structure to the existing find branch):
   ```c
   struct model_entry *e = model_find(&m, keybuf);
   int rc = rb_delete(t, keybuf);
   if (e == NULL) {
       if (rc != -1) { /* fprintf + return 1: rb_delete succeeded on an absent key */ }
   } else {
       if (rc != 0) { /* fprintf + return 1: rb_delete failed on a key that exists */ }
       model_delete(&m, keybuf);
       if (rb_find(t, keybuf) != NULL) { /* fprintf + return 1: key still findable post-delete */ }
   }
   ```
   This checks both directions of the contract (spec's ownership section, and
   `include/rbtree.h`'s comment on `rb_delete`): absent key -> `-1`, tree unchanged; present key
   -> `0`, and the key is now genuinely gone from the tree, not just from the model.

4. **Everything else is untouched and just starts covering delete for free**: the periodic
   `rb_validate` (now also catching any `delete_fixup` black-height regression), and the
   post-op `rb_size(t) == m.count` check (now also catching an off-by-one from a botched
   splice or a missed `t->size--`), already run unconditionally every iteration regardless of
   which branch fired.

No changes anywhere in `src/rbtree.c` -- this is purely a test-harness change.

## Why this specifically closes last turn's flagged gap

With inserts and deletes both drawn from the same 5000-key space over 100k+ ops, the tree will
naturally grow, shrink, and get restructured through long chains of rotations from both
`insert_fixup` and `delete_fixup` -- producing exactly the deep, multi-level `delete_fixup`
Case-3 climbs (and eventually a climb that reaches the actual root) that the 9 hand-picked
table cases can't reach by construction. Any bug there surfaces either as an `rb_validate`
failure (invariant 3, black-height) within 100 ops of when it happened, or as a
tree/model/size disagreement immediately.

## Verification

1. `make test` -- now runs `./build/fuzz 100000` doing a real mix of insert/find/delete;
   expect `fuzz: 100000 insert/find/delete ops OK` (update the success message to say
   "insert/find/delete" instead of "insert/find").
2. `make asan` -- same run under ASan/UBSan.
3. `make memcheck` -- valgrind run at the existing lower op count (20000, already set in the
   Makefile for speed under valgrind's overhead).
4. Re-run a few times with different seeds (the fuzzer already accepts an optional seed as
   `argv[2]`) to get variety across runs, same as it already supports today.
